explanation:
0 — you’re not in the wrong for saying she went back on a promise.

She told you not to worry and said they would cover anything the car needed besides gas, so treating a needed repair like a Christmas gift is a change from what she originally promised. Your frustration makes sense because this wasn’t some extra upgrade; it was a repair on the car you were relying on. You did raise your voice and make a pointed comparison, which didn’t help, but that doesn’t change the basic issue: she said one thing and then tried to reframe it later. The fact that she raised her voice too only made the argument worse, not your point less true.

Her side would probably be that the divorce changed the money situation and that she sees paying for the repair as still helping you, even if she labels it differently.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

You said you planned to make hot dogs for lunch, not that you wanted your mom to make them right then. She chose to prepare them without checking timing with you first, and then yelled at you over “wasting food,” which is unfair. You also weren’t refusing to be difficult; you had just brushed your teeth and hadn’t agreed on when lunch was happening. And you did recognize that she was trying to do something nice and made them the way you like, which shows you weren’t being rude for no reason.

Your mom would probably say she was trying to help and felt unappreciated after putting in the effort.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. Being upset about getting woken up at 5:30 by a blow dryer when your alarm is 6:15 is reasonable. She changed a routine that used to work for both of you, and a loud hair dryer that early can fairly be seen as disruptive. You also are not talking about banning her routine; you’re describing a small fix, like asking her to wait a bit or you adjusting a little too. And from what you wrote, there was no clear rule or promise either of you broke, so this is more a household scheduling problem than anyone doing something awful.

Her side might be that mornings are the only practical time for her workout and getting ready, so waiting longer could throw off her whole routine.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

Your concern is about his health, not about trying to control him, and you were honest that you are not even sure whether he is addicted. He is 17, the smoking has been getting more frequent, and that makes it more serious than a one-off bad choice. The family history of lung cancer also makes this a real reason to speak up, not just gossiping or meddling. And right now you have only considered telling your parents; you have not actually gone behind his back or tried to blow up his life.

Your brother might say it is his business, that he is almost an adult, and that telling your parents would feel like betrayal.

You are the asshole for looking at her butt.

The main issue is the specific action: you chose to look at a stranger’s body in a sexual way instead of just looking away. Even if it was brief, people notice that kind of thing, and it can make someone feel watched or uncomfortable. The fact that her friends reacted right away suggests it came across clearly enough to bother them. “She was standing there” does not really change that, because noticing someone is different from checking out their body.

The other side might say it was only a quick glance and not meant to be creepy, but from their view it still looked disrespectful.

0 — you were not in the wrong.

Your employer kept rejecting work because the icons looked pixelated when viewed enlarged, even though the issue was the small size of the assets, not that you made them badly. You tried to explain the technical limit, then restated it in simpler terms so she could understand, which sounds like an effort to communicate, not talk down to her. She still didn’t seem to get it, but she eventually forwarded the work to front end, which suggests the point got across enough to move the project forward. Based on what you described, this reads more like clarifying a misunderstanding than “mansplaining.”

The other side might say that phrases like “dumbed it down” can come off as condescending even if your explanation itself was accurate.

0 — you are not in the wrong.

A polite text asking him to turn it down is a normal first step when a repeated noise is affecting your sleep and making your home stressful. You also did not jump straight to blaming him; you spent time trying to figure out whether it was AC, another neighbor, or something else first. The sound has been going on for hours over multiple nights, so this is not a one-time minor annoyance. And you are talking about a calm request, not picking a fight or retaliating.

What the other side might say: he may not realize the sound carries upstairs or that it is bothering you, so he could prefer a friendly heads-up first.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

You said clearly that adding this new player made the game less fun for you: it messed up the balance, forced extra grinding, and turned late-game progress into carrying someone who wouldn’t listen. That’s a fair reason to not want to keep playing in the same group.

You also did communicate your problem instead of just blowing up or shutting everyone out. Your friend kept pushing his other friend into the game anyway, even after you explained why it was frustrating.

On top of that, you weren’t stopping them from playing entirely — you even let them keep using your server while you were AFK. That makes this more about protecting your own enjoyment than controlling theirs.

The other side might say they just wanted to include a newer player and thought you could be more patient.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

Your boyfriend waved her over and then spent about an hour talking with her while you were left out, which is a pretty fair reason to feel upset on a night that was supposed to be about the two of you. On top of that, when you wanted to leave, he made it worse by getting mad and calling your reaction a “pissy attitude” instead of noticing you’d been sidelined. Even if he and his ex are on good terms because they share a child, that doesn’t make it okay to ignore you in that setting.

That said, you probably had a better option than tugging him away and then sitting on your phone; saying plainly, “I’m uncomfortable and feel left out,” would have made your point clearer.

From his side, he might say he was just being friendly and keeping things civil with the mother of his child.

0 — you are not in the wrong.

You are not sharing drinks when you have an active cold sore, and you said you follow the usual precautions, which is the main practical issue here. HSV-1 is also very common, and you are not required to announce a personal health detail to a group every time people joke about it. On top of that, the “you don’t have herpes, do you?” comments put you on the spot in public, so it makes sense that you did not want to answer that in front of everyone. Also, based on what you wrote, there is no actual harm described from your choice not to disclose.

The other side might say that, since they directly joked about not wanting exposure, being clearer by simply refusing to share drinks or addressing it privately would avoid mixed signals.

0 — you are not in the wrong.

You are already carrying a heavy load by helping care for your dad while also raising and homeschooling two young kids. That is a real contribution, not something selfish or unreasonable.

From your account, the problem is not that you caused a family rupture, but that your sister dismissed your caregiving as “stupid” and resisted helping because she would rather use that time for leisure. That is very different from trying to solve the situation fairly.

You also describe your sister persuading your mom to stop helping, which made your dad’s care worse and increased the conflict. That points to their choices escalating things, not you simply asking for support.

And calling your efforts “stupid” is not a constructive way to handle a hard family crisis.

The other side might say they are overwhelmed, burned out, or feel the hospital should be handling more of his care.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You’re not in the wrong for feeling uncomfortable about a two-week trip with someone you’ve only met twice. That’s a long time to travel closely with a group, and it’s reasonable to wish the plans had been checked with everyone first. You also weren’t cruel about her—you said she seems nice and sweet, and your issue is more about group comfort and your own shyness than about her as a person. On top of that, you were willing to stay optimistic and not let your anxiety turn into drama, which matters.

The other side might say it’s his sister’s trip too, the friend may fit in fine, and there’s still time to get more comfortable before July.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. If they are letting people assume they’re very involved when they go months without calling or visiting, you would not be wrong to correct that.

A few reasons. First, this is not just about your hurt feelings: your daughter notices the absence and is asking why they do not come around. Second, you did try the fair route already by talking to your mom and sister multiple times and by bringing your daughter to see them, and nothing changed. Third, being honest about the current situation is different from attacking them, especially if they are using holiday photos and vague comments to give a false picture.

At the same time, it is worth remembering they did help a lot for years with childcare, and your mom’s illness was real, so calling it out should stay factual and not erase that past help.

They might say their health, energy, or personal issues make regular contact harder than it looks from the outside.

Yes — you would be the asshole if you told your manager she smells after handling it this way.

First, you’ve already let this become workplace gossip instead of a respectful, private concern, and that makes it more hurtful. Second, the way you describe her odor is harsh and personal, which suggests telling her yourself could come out badly even if you mean well. Third, because she is your manager, this is better handled through a professional channel like HR or another supervisor, not by an employee confronting her directly. And while the smell is clearly affecting coworkers, that still doesn’t make a blunt personal comment from you the right move.

To your credit, you did try not to embarrass her in the moment by not reacting visibly.

She might say she’d rather be told than have people talk about her behind her back, but that still doesn’t make your direct confrontation the best way to handle it now.

Yes, you would be the asshole if you told your niece to “shut up.”

“Shut up” is harsher than the situation calls for, especially when the only issue you named is that she’s generally loud. Wanting a calmer birthday is fair, but speaking to her that way would be rude and more likely to hurt her feelings than solve the problem. You also have a better option: ask her politely to use a quieter voice or have someone else help manage the noise. The problem is not wanting peace on your birthday; it’s the specific way you’re thinking of saying it.

Your niece’s side would probably be that she wasn’t trying to ruin your day, she was just being her usual loud self, and being told to “shut up” would feel mean.

1 — you were in the wrong for publicly talking about your ex’s genitals and sex life in front of mutual friends.

First, that was private information, and he clearly looked embarrassed and unhappy the moment you said it. Second, your comment directly led to catcalling, cheering, and someone grabbing him, which made the situation worse. Third, when he told you privately that it bothered him, you didn’t really own it—you said it was “totally different for a guy” and that you were “just trying to help” instead of respecting his boundary. Fourth, telling him to “calm down” after he was already upset usually makes people feel more dismissed, not heard.

He might say that even if you meant it as a compliment, you shared intimate details without his consent and then brushed off his feelings when he told you it crossed a line.

1 — you were in the wrong for staying at the wedding until midnight after telling your wife you’d only go to the ceremony and come right home.

First, you made a clear plan for your anniversary and then completely changed it without telling her. Second, she was home with three kids, expecting you back, so your silence left her stuck and worried for hours. Third, “no service inside” doesn’t really cover it when you chose to stay all day and night; if your plans changed that much, it was on you to step outside and send one update. Fourth, the fact that she had to call a mutual friend shows how out of the loop you left her.

From her side, this probably looks less like missing a message and more like you blew off your wife, your family plans, and your anniversary.

YTA for knocking over and breaking a microwave, toaster, and boxes of bowls and lids at work.

Your boss handled your birthday shift badly, especially after you gave three weeks’ notice and had plans, but that does not make destroying property okay. You escalated things twice: first by getting into a heated argument, and then by taking it out on equipment and supplies. You had better options, like refusing to stay, leaving, or raising the issue calmly with the manager afterward instead of causing damage. The fact that you now feel bad and accept paying for what you broke shows some self-awareness, but it does not change that your specific action was out of line.

The other side would probably say the injury still had to be dealt with in the moment and that your reaction made a staffing problem much worse.

You are in the wrong for refusing to stop for your daughter’s birthday donut and turning it into a comment on her weight and eating.

First, she is 19, and this was a small, reasonable birthday treat after doing an activity you wanted on her birthday. Second, you did not just say no to a stop; you policed her calories, doubted what she said about the donut, and brought up cake she “would probably” eat later. That makes it less about the stop and more about controlling her food. Third, you had a better option: either make the quick stop or simply decline without criticizing her body and diet.

Your daughter also kept the argument going after you said no and brought her mother into it afterward, which did not help. But that does not change that your choice was the main problem.

From her side, this likely felt less like concern for her health and more like being shamed over one donut on her birthday.

1 — You were in the wrong for lying about the invite and for the way you spoke to him.

First, you discussed the party right in front of him, then said you might add him, and didn’t. That gave him false hope instead of a clear answer. Second, telling him to “f*ck off and stop being an annoying c*nt” at the airport was needlessly harsh and escalated things way beyond “we don’t click.”  
Third, you were allowed not to invite him, but once you chose that, the fair thing was to be direct and polite, not vague in public and then exclude him anyway. Finally, his pushing to be included was annoying, but it doesn’t excuse cruelty or mixed signals from you.

His side would probably be that he was trying too hard to fit in, but you made it more hurtful by insulting him and implying he still had a chance to come.

You are in the wrong for taking your niece’s keychain twice without permission.

First, it was her gift, not a spare household item, and you took it even after she had already made it clear she wanted it back. Second, finding it hidden in her pouch and taking it again crossed a bigger line, because you knew she did not consent. Third, going through her things and throwing some of them out while “cleaning” was not your call. Finally, “I need it more” does not make it yours, and gifts, money, or snacks you offered before do not buy access to her property.

Her reaction was not great either: yelling, grabbing it, and throwing your car key across the room was wrong.

From her side, she would probably say this was never about how useful the keychain was; it was about you taking something personal from a kid who already felt pushed out of her own space.

1 — you’re in the wrong for pushing your girlfriend to cancel the tattoo appointment.

First, it’s her body, so the final choice about tattoos is hers, even if you strongly dislike them. Second, being “a team” does not mean you get veto power over her appearance; it means you each respect the other’s autonomy. Third, your argument leans on fear that one meaningful tattoo will turn into “many meaningless ones,” which is speculation, not a fair reason to control this decision. Fourth, she already knows your view, and repeating it to pressure her into canceling crosses from having a preference into trying to manage her choices.

From her side, she’d probably say she heard your opinion, but she should still be free to make a personal decision about her own body without being made to feel guilty.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

1. You were wrong for telling your boss a misleading story that could damage this person’s chance at the job.

First, you were the one in a relationship, had the emotional affair, and even tried to make it physical, so shifting the blame onto them was unfair. Second, when your boss pressed you, you didn’t just keep a boundary or refuse to comment—you gave a one-sided version that made them look uniquely unethical. Third, you used private history to influence a hiring decision for your own comfort, not because of anything work-related. Fourth, even if they also made bad choices, that doesn’t justify you presenting the situation in a distorted way.

The other side might say they knowingly got involved with someone taken and that your discomfort was real, but that still doesn’t make it okay to mislead your boss.

1 — You were in the wrong for repeatedly mocking your friend to force a response.

First, you made it personal: memes, calling him a clown, and bringing up his partner’s meth use whenever he mentioned sex crossed the line from concern into humiliation. Second, you had a better option and chose not to use it. If you were worried, you could have spoken to him directly and respectfully about what you heard instead of trying to bait him. Third, your goal was to provoke him, not to help, and that usually just makes people shut down or get defensive. Finally, the fact that you apologized later is good, but it also shows you know your behavior was the problem.

From his side, he’d probably say you took a rumor or secondhand information and used it to publicly embarrass him instead of acting like a friend.

You are not the asshole.

It’s reasonable to be annoyed when the same person posts the exact same meme across several subreddits you follow, because that can clutter your feed with duplicates. Their reason—wanting more people to see it—does make sense, but it doesn’t change the fact that it creates a worse experience for people who follow multiple meme communities. So your opinion that people shouldn’t do it is fair.

The only caution is that calling them out directly can turn a small annoyance into an argument, especially when they already have a stock answer and are not likely to stop. That doesn’t make you wrong for disliking it; it just means confronting them may not help much.

The other side would say they are just trying to reach different audiences, and that reposting to multiple subreddits is normal on Reddit.

You were in the wrong for shoving your brother’s head away and bluntly telling him not to put his face in your boobs.

He did start unusual physical contact without asking, and it makes sense that you were startled by him grabbing your waist and burying his face there. But the part that crossed the line was your reaction: shoving his head away was harsher than it needed to be. You had better options in the moment, like pulling your body back, moving seats, or calmly saying “don’t do that” without making it more intense. Your blunt wording also escalated the embarrassment and is probably why he cried and the whole room got awkward.

That said, your boundary itself was fair: he should not have put his face there without consent, even if he was scared.

From his side, he’d probably say he was frightened during the movie, reached for comfort without thinking, and felt hurt by how forcefully you pushed him away.

1 — You were in the wrong for telling your sister to “suck a cabbage.”

Your actual request to your mum was fair: if she already knows she can only take you at a certain time, it would be clearer to say that first instead of asking which train you want and then overruling it. That was a practical point, not an attack.

The problem is how it ended. Once your sister called you rude, you escalated the situation with an insult instead of keeping it about the communication issue. That shifted things away from the real problem and made you look worse.

Also, your mum is doing you a daily favor by driving you, so even when her way of asking is annoying, it matters to stay respectful when you raise it.

Your sister might say your tone at dinner and the insult made a simple conversation into unnecessary drama.

0 — you’re not in the wrong for being frustrated.

First, being woken up every day at 7 a.m. by a loud argument and a tantrum right under your bedroom window would wear on most people, especially when it cuts two hours off your sleep. Second, your neighbour knows your work hours and that you’re a light sleeper, so having that discussion in that exact spot does come across as inconsiderate. Third, you haven’t lashed out or tried to start trouble; you’ve handled it quietly by shutting the window and trying to go back to sleep. Frustration is not the same thing as bad behavior.

The other side might say 7 a.m. is a normal time for families to leave for kindergarten and that young kids can be noisy, even when parents are trying to manage them.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You’re not in the wrong for pulling back from plans when being around these friends leaves you feeling worse.

First, they’re making jokes at your expense about your school and living at home, and that’s not harmless if it keeps hurting you. Second, it makes sense that you’d cancel when you already expect to come home feeling awful after seeing them. Third, the bigger issue isn’t that you don’t care about them; it’s that the dynamic with them is making social time feel unsafe instead of supportive.

What does matter is that repeatedly saying yes and then cancelling will frustrate people, so if you can, it would be better to stop agreeing to plans you already think you won’t want to keep.

They might say the cancellations feel unreliable or rude, especially if they don’t realize how much their comments are affecting you.

1 — You were in the wrong for calling Sally and telling her to stop parenting the kids and to keep her family at a distance.

First, you are relying on her a lot: childcare, rides, school runs, photos, house-viewing help, and even borrowed money. It’s unfair to accept all that support and then attack her for being involved.

Second, she is doing the day-to-day work of helping raise the children where they live: meals, reading, school support, transport, and making space for them at home. That is parenting, even if you are still their mother.

Third, you didn’t calmly set a boundary. You escalated it by saying she had “no relation” to them, objecting to her school involvement, and policing what the kids call her parents.

Fourth, your issue seems to be about feeling replaced, but the kids benefiting from another caring adult is not a bad thing.

Sally and Jim would probably say that if she is helping raise the kids every day, she cannot be treated like a stranger when it suits you.

0 — you are not in the wrong.

You did take the concern seriously and pushed your mom to say something instead of just shrugging it off. After that, Cathy was told Sean might need follow-up for possible Marfan syndrome, so the information did get to the person who needed to hear it. Once she reportedly brushed it off, that became her choice, not your failure. Also, this was a very sensitive medical issue involving people you barely knew, so not feeling comfortable stepping in directly was reasonable.

What the other side might say is that because the risk sounded so serious, you should have told Cathy yourself before her return trip instead of relying on your mom.

1 — You would be the asshole if you brought kids with the flu to family Christmas before the contagious period was clearly over.

First, flu can still spread even after a fever is gone, so “no fever” is not a safe rule by itself. Second, Christmas is a family event with lots of close contact, which makes passing it around much more likely. Third, your sister already made it clear she does not want that risk, and that boundary should be respected. Fourth, other relatives could be vulnerable even if they seem healthy, and they should not be exposed without their consent.

Your side is that you genuinely misunderstood how long flu stays contagious and were using the fever rule, but that still would not make it okay to bring them.

0 — you are not in the wrong.

First, it’s your home and your internet, and guests are not entitled to automatic phone wifi access, especially when they already have call, text, and data options. Second, the real problem here was your friend’s behavior: they kept ranting about it and turned a small comment into a public scene at your party. Third, that made the atmosphere uncomfortable enough that someone else had to step in and calm things down, which is not reasonable over wifi. Finally, you handled the feedback well afterward by recognizing the communication issue and looking into guest wifi for the future.

What the other side might say is that wifi feels normal to offer now and that not sharing it can come across as oddly strict or unwelcoming, even if it’s still your choice.

You are the asshole for routinely driving well above the speed limit and passing people on the right to keep your speed up.

First, passing on the right is less expected, so it makes your moves harder for other drivers to predict. Second, you’re choosing not to slow down or adjust when traffic patterns call for it, especially near on-ramps where people are merging and already dealing with limited space and timing. Third, your own explanation is basically that you do this because braking or changing lanes would interrupt the pace you want, and that puts your preference over safety. Fourth, the fact that other drivers may be sitting in the wrong lane does not make your response safer.

The other side might say lane campers create the problem and merging drivers should judge gaps better, but that still doesn’t make speeding and right-side passing the safer choice.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0.

Those are serious issues, and raising concern about them is not wrong in itself. The bigger problem is the setting: your SO’s workplace award night is not a fair or useful place to drop serious allegations. It also matters that what you’ve found is about her company, not clear proof that she personally used child labour or personally caused the environmental damage. And while her bragging and nasty attitude may make you dislike her, that is separate from whether this is the right moment to confront her.

Her side would probably say you were using a work event to embarrass her over claims that should be raised privately or in a better setting.

1 — you are in the wrong for choosing an optional trip over being there for your 12-year-old daughter’s birthday.

First, this is not an emergency or something unavoidable; it’s a want, and you’re picking it over a day that matters to your child now. Second, you were given a reasonable compromise: leave later or shorten the trip so you could still catch part of the concert and be present for her birthday, and you refused it. Third, saying she’ll “get over it” and that there will be other birthdays dismisses her feelings. Kids remember when a parent treats their milestone like it is less important than entertainment. Fourth, a makeup party is not the same as having her parent there on the actual day, especially at 12.

The other side might say this concert feels rare and meaningful to you and your son, but that still doesn’t make missing your younger daughter’s birthday the right choice.

You are in the wrong for telling your wife to wait and then pushing a home metal-detector test instead of getting your toddler promptly checked for a possible swallowed coin.

First, with an 18-month-old, “he seems fine right now” does not rule out a real problem, and waiting until after work added delay. Second, your idea was mainly about avoiding the cost of x-rays, but at that point it was not a medically confirmed substitute for an exam. Third, your wife had a reasonable reason to act fast because she only suspected the coin and did not know where it was or whether it could cause trouble. Fourth, even though you were trying to solve the problem, your plan put your own experiment ahead of the safer option in the moment.

Your side is that you were not trying to ignore it, and you thought you had a practical way to check before paying for treatment.

1 — you were in the wrong for looking her up on Facebook and telling her parents about her dating profile.

First, nothing in your story says she lied to you, threatened you, or broke a rule. If you weren’t comfortable dating her, you could have simply not seen her again. Second, you went outside the app, found her private social media, and involved her parents in her dating life. That was a major invasion of privacy. Third, if you truly thought there was a problem, the fair option was to use the site’s moderation tools, not decide on your own that she couldn’t make dating choices. Fourth, the site banning you for three months strongly suggests your actions crossed clear boundaries there too.

The other side would likely say they were trying to protect her, but concern doesn’t give you the right to investigate her and report her to her parents.

You are not in the wrong.

The biggest reason is that they offered you a free pizza, let you come back and order, and only then revoked it at checkout. That’s unfair, because you relied on the deal they already gave you. If they wanted to withdraw it because of your earlier message, they should have told you right away, not after your pizza was being made.

Also, your complaint to corporate was about the store making one promise and then backing out later, which is what happened twice from your point of view. It makes sense that you were upset about being left scrambling for food and then embarrassed at the register.

That said, your text to the store was over the line. Swearing at employees and then arguing at checkout did not help your case, and saying they had a “habit” of this based on one incident was a stretch.

The other side would say they canceled the free pizza because of your abusive message and did not want to reward that behavior.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

You said you didn’t want to meet or talk to this friend, and that should have been respected instead of repeatedly being pushed. Your reason also wasn’t random: you have anxiety, and this specific situation ties into a fear about his ex through someone connected to her. You also explained your concern clearly instead of just refusing with no context, so he knew exactly why you were uncomfortable. His reassurances may have been well meant, but reassurance is not the same as respecting a boundary.

He might say he only wanted everyone to get along and was trying to help you feel safer by telling you the friend doesn’t hate you.

1 — you were in the wrong for deliberately building fake “mutual friends” and then lying that it was a coincidence.

First, this was not just casually looking someone up after a party. You spent a week adding people from his network and joining their groups specifically to get closer to him. Second, you then hid that plan by telling him Facebook just suggested him and that the mutual friends happened naturally, which was dishonest. Third, he said he’d be right back at the party and didn’t return, so pushing ahead through his social circle instead of contacting him plainly ignored that social cue. Finally, changing your interests around his shows and music to create more overlap makes the whole approach feel more manufactured than romantic.

From his side, he might say that if you had simply sent him a direct message after the party, it would have felt honest, while the behind-the-scenes effort and lie would feel unsettling if he knew.

1 — you were in the wrong for secretly taking on extra unpaid work, then using that hidden sacrifice against her after the breakup.

First, you made a big relationship decision on your own. Even if your goal was to see her more later, the plan also made you less available in the short term, which was already a problem.

Second, because you kept it a surprise, she had no chance to understand it, support it, or plan around it. You can’t expect appreciation for effort the other person never knew was happening.

Third, there was a better option: tell her what you were doing and talk about whether it actually helped the relationship. That would have made it a joint plan instead of a private sacrifice.

Finally, bringing it up afterward came off like guilt-tripping. Since she never asked for it, it was unfair to make her feel responsible for your choice.

Her side would be that distance and time were real issues, and your secret plan made those issues worse before it could ever help.

Yes — you would be the asshole for asking your brother not to bring his husband to your wedding because of your fiancée’s homophobic family.

First, you’d be excluding a married spouse for who he is, not because he did anything wrong. Second, that puts the burden of other people’s prejudice on your brother and his husband, which is unfair and likely very hurtful. Third, saying you “have nothing against him” doesn’t really fix it when the result is still treating his marriage as less acceptable than everyone else’s relationships. Finally, the problem here is your fiancée’s relatives’ behavior, not your brother’s husband’s presence.

I get that you want a peaceful wedding, but choosing to accommodate the homophobic people by excluding the gay spouse is still the harmful choice.

The other side would likely say it’s your wedding and you’re trying to avoid drama, but avoiding drama by shutting out your brother’s husband is exactly why this would be wrong.

You are not the asshole.

You forgot the footpath rules, but forgetting them and being too far ahead to warn your husband is not the same thing as causing the collision on purpose. The adult who was actually with your son at the time had the chance to watch where they were going and manage where the child was walking. Also, even if your husband and son were on the wrong side, that still does not make it okay for a cyclist to hit a child and respond by yelling instead of checking if he was hurt.
